rationale: Reselected onto participant eligibility after closing the read-index thread. The claim under test is that a node removed from the configuration can still have its proposals accepted, contradicting node.go's own stated intent to block proposals from a removed node. Two source facts make it concrete: node.run() disables the proposal channel when the node learns it was removed (setting propc to nil) but re-enables it on any observed leader change, with the in-tree comment conceding that this is 'not very sound and likely has bugs'; and neither the leader's MsgProp handler nor the follower's forwarding path checks whether the sender is still a member. A focused probe against the real FSM confirms both halves: after applyConfChange removed node 3 from a leader's config (voters became [1 2], Progress[3] deleted), stepping a MsgProp with From=3 was accepted with err=nil and appended one entry; and a removed follower still forwarded a local MsgProp to its leader. I record this as a new sourced question with an open discriminator rather than as an asserted defect, because whether the library owes sender-eligibility or the application owns that authorization is exactly what is unsettled.

investigations.question: Can a node that the configuration no longer contains have its proposals accepted and committed after it learns of a new leader? node.run() blocks the proposal channel only until the next observed leader change, and describes that behaviour as unsound; do the raft handlers then accept a proposal whose sender is not a member, and is sender eligibility a library duty or a caller duty?
investigations.hypothesis: The Node facade re-enables the proposal channel whenever lead != r.lead and the new lead is not None, regardless of the node's own membership, so a removed node's client can keep proposing after any leadership change; the proposal is then forwarded by stepFollower to the current leader, and stepLeader's MsgProp handler writes it without consulting Progress[m.From], so the entry is appended and can be committed even though the sender is not in the configuration.
investigations.discriminator: Decide who owns sender eligibility: if the library's documented contract places authorization on the caller (the application), then accepting a proposal from a non-member is out of scope and the suspicion is refuted; if node.go's own stated intent to block proposals from a removed node is the contract, then re-enabling the channel on a leader change is a defect. Concretely: check whether any handler or contract rejects MsgProp from an id absent from the configuration, and whether the application can observe that its request came from a removed member.

knowledge.statement: Proposal eligibility handling in this snapshot. In node.run, the proposal send channel is set to nil when the node learns that it was removed from the configuration by a config change it applied (only when it was in the config before), which blocks incoming proposals, but it is re-assigned to the real channel whenever the observed leader changes to a non-None value, independently of the node's membership; the accompanying in-tree comment states that this is not sound and likely has bugs. On the raft side, stepFollower's MsgProp case forwards the message to r.lead without any membership test, and stepLeader's MsgProp case only checks whether the leader itself is still a member (Progress[r.id] == nil) before appending, so a proposal whose From is not in the configuration is written to the log if it reaches the leader.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the Node facade (the goroutine-driven run loop) plus the raft handlers; RawNode users bypass the facade and step messages directly, and DisableProposalForwarding only affects followers that are members. The behaviour concerns eligibility of the proposer, not voting or commit quorums, which continue to use the configuration.

gaps.question: Does any part of the library contract, node documentation or Ready/Propose API make sender eligibility the caller's responsibility (so that a leader accepting a non-member's proposal is intended), or is node.go's 'block incoming proposals' the intended guarantee, which the leader-change path then breaks?

knowledge.assertion: the proposal channel is re-enabled on leader change regardless of membership, and neither the follower forward path nor the leader append path checks sender membership

interpretations.rationale: Source account plus one focused probe (native feedback only; no retained receipt). Sources establish the mechanism: node.run's lead-change branch re-assigns propc on any transition to a non-None leader, while the removal branch sets it to nil only at the moment the removal is applied and is accompanied by an in-tree comment admitting the logic is unsound; stepFollower's MsgProp case forwards to r.lead unconditionally; stepLeader's MsgProp case checks only the leader's own membership. The probe drove the real FSM directly: with voters {1,2,3}, a leader that applied a ConfChange removing node 3 reported voters [1 2] with Progress[3] deleted, and yet stepping a MsgProp with From=3 returned nil and appended one entry (lastIndex 1 to 2); a separate instance for node 3, made a follower of node 2 and then made to apply its own removal, still forwarded a local MsgProp to node 2. So the raft-level half of the hypothesis is confirmed, and the facade half follows from the source reading. Why this stays unresolved rather than asserted: the decisive question is ownership of sender eligibility. Raft's contract is about replication and commit quorums; a proposal is data to be replicated, and the library documents that proposals can be lost and that the caller must retry, but it does not document that raft authorizes the proposer. If authorization belongs to the application, then the leader appending a non-member's entry is not a defect - the application chose to forward it - and node.go's comment is only about a local convenience; if the intent really is to block proposals from a removed node, then the leader-change re-enablement is a defect because it silently revives a channel the code deliberately closed. I did not let the probe settle that, and I did not weaken the question by treating the comment as proof of the intended contract. Counterevidence and limits: (a) RawNode users bypass the facade entirely and can step any MsgProp, which supports the caller-owns-authorization reading; (b) DisableProposalForwarding exists precisely so an operator can stop members from forwarding, implying forwarding by members is normal and by non-members is a configuration concern; (c) the removal branch checks okBefore so a node that never knew it was a member is not blocked; (d) my probe modified no production logic and used only public/package-internal entry points. The gap above records what would settle it, and the behaviour is recorded as a fact without a defect judgment.
limitations: The probe is native feedback, not a retained receipt; the observation it produced is described here and in the behaviour fact rather than cited by check id.
The facade half (propc re-enablement) is established by source reading, not by driving a live Node goroutine through a removal followed by a leader change.
No downstream usage (etcd) was examined to see whether applications rely on the leader for sender authorization.
Severity is not assessed because the ownership question is open; no data-integrity or safety consequence is claimed.
